title: Private Information Pricing System Based on Game Theory and Graph Theory

source.relative_path: 2018美赛特等奖/F题4篇/F83744-Private Information Pricing System Based on Game Theory and Graph Theory.pdf

context_sources.name: Acquisti, the economics of personal data and privacy
Shapley, a value for n-person games
Dohmen et al., individual risk attitudes, SOEP
Barabasi and Albert, emergence of scaling

limitations: The worked finance example is flattened, though the result 0.326 is legible.
The three comparison matrices are devised by the authors and their entries are not printed.
The government price is called a Shapley value without the coalition arithmetic.
The appendix scores do not match the printed formula: 4/15 times ln 4 is not 0.29.
The polynomial fit of willingness is given without a goodness-of-fit measure.

tasks: Define private information and price its disclosure risk
Measure the amount of information in a bundle
Find the price that clears a two-stage game
Decide when privacy is a right and when it is traded
Let the value decay with time and vary with age
Model a large breach and the response
Extend to a network and set a corrective tax

section_map.summary: A two-stage game extended by a scale-free network.
Seven recommendations, from price to a matched tax.
A definition, and a lease rather than a sale.
Three sub-risks, hierarchy weights, one worked number.
Entropy rejected; completeness times a logarithm.
Sell or steal, then the midpoint price.
Rights, decay, age perception, a breach.
10,000 nodes, a swept tax, welfare rising with the side effect.
Two bundles scored, Bob above Alice.

contributions.summary: One price interval that gives three regimes as the pricing power moves.
A punishment bound that sorts a ban from light supervision.
A tax searched over a grid, matched to the sign of the side effect.

dependency_graph.handoff: The disclosure risk and the information amount set the gains and the risk inside the game
The two equilibrium conditions are what time, age and a breach are tested against
The person's payoff in the game becomes the node's payoff on the network

assumptions.summary: Three parties, perfect information, no resale, and the government sets the price.
Profitable records are worth nothing without the basic identifying ones.
Relationships run both ways and well-connected people attract more links.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Fraud insurance priced at 9.9 CNY, about 1.57 dollars, from named products.
Median willingness to take risks by age, from the SOEP survey.
Gains and risks drawn uniformly on the unit interval for 10,000 nodes.

models.summary: Three weighted sub-risks and a logarithmic amount.
A two-period game with the price at the midpoint.
Linear and exponential decay, plus an age index.
Disclosure on a scale-free network with a corrective tax.

verification.summary: One worked finance case gives a risk of 0.326.
The sweeps reproduce the expected direction: tax the harm, subsidize the help.

results_trace.summary: Finance weights (0.57, 0.34, 0.08) give a risk of 0.326.
At age 30 the willingness score is 5.94 and the index is 0.4678.
Best welfare rises with the side effect; the best tax falls as it turns positive.

writing_logic.summary: The game is told as a sequence before any payoff.
The price window is shown to be narrow before the point is chosen.
A breach is first a failure, then a repair, then a return to normal.

language_observations.summary: Three ideas share one trait and differ in one that matters.
A standard method is tried and dropped for a named reason.
The question is answered by splitting it into two levels.
Six limits are owned, each with its cause.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: the decision tree of the baseline game.
Figure 2: supply and demand for the records.
Figure 3: willingness to take risks against age.
Figure 4: the generated network of 10,000 nodes.
Figure 5: welfare against the tax at a negative side effect.
Figure 6: welfare against the tax at a positive side effect.
Figure 7: maximum welfare against the side effect.
Figure 8: the best tax against the side effect.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The midpoint is labelled a Shapley value without the coalition sum.
The comparison matrices are devised by the authors, not elicited.
The two sample scores do not follow the printed formula.

weaknesses.summary: No imperfect information, no robustness check, subjective parameter forms, one-to-one trades only, protection costs ignored, and no time for the resale effect.
The gains are never written as functions of the amount of information.
The network result rests on one draw and fixed parameters.

independent_extensions.summary: Relax perfect information and let parameters be learned.
Specify the two gains as functions of the amount.
Repeat the sweep over many network draws.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Force the data holder to repay misuse or loss, to remove the moral hazard.
Match the tax or subsidy to the size and sign of the side effect.

unresolved_questions.question: What functions link the two gains to the amount of information?
What entries were used in the three comparison matrices?
What decay rate and half-life fit real records?
